stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Marriage is a special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman entered into in accordance with law for the establishment of conjugal and family life.

2. The nature, consequences and incidents of marriage are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except that marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage without any limitation.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: FC Art. 1. No. 1 is the first sentence of Art. 1 verbatim, so it is true. No. 2 is false because Art. 1 allows marriage settlements to fix the property relations during the marriage only 'within the limits provided by this Code'. Marriage settlements are subject to Arts. 74-81 (e.g., they cannot be contrary to law, morals or public policy). Tolentino notes that marriage is a special contract because, unlike ordinary contracts, its nature, consequences and incidents are fixed by law and it cannot be terminated by the parties' agreement.

stem: A couple executes a prenuptial agreement which principally provides that their marriage shall be valid for only 5 years but that it can be renewed through mutual consent negotiated at least 6 months before its expiration. Is this contract valid?
choices: Yes, because future spouses may stipulate on any matter in their marriage settlement.
Yes, provided the agreement is in writing and registered.
No, because marriage is a permanent union whose nature and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation, except property relations.
No, because prenuptial agreements must be executed after the marriage.
explanation: FC Art. 1: marriage is a special contract of PERMANENT union, and its nature, consequences and incidents are governed by law and not subject to stipulation. The only exception is that marriage settlements may fix the property relations during the marriage within the limits of the Code (see also Arts. 74-75). A stipulation that the marriage lasts only five years, renewable by mutual consent, attempts to fix the duration and dissolution of the marriage by agreement. It is void. Choice a ignores the Art. 1 exception's limit to property relations, and d is wrong because marriage settlements must be executed BEFORE the celebration of the marriage (Art. 76).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A man and a woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are conclusively presumed to have entered into a lawful contract of marriage.
2. In case of doubt, all presumptions favor the solidarity of the family; thus, every intendment of law or facts leans toward the validity of marriage and the indissolubility of the marriage bonds.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false because Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa) of the Rules of Court makes this a DISPUTABLE presumption ('satisfactory if uncontradicted, but may be contradicted and overcome by other evidence'), not a conclusive one. No. 2 is true: it reproduces Civil Code Art. 220. Together these reflect the policy of Art. XV, Sec. 2 of the Constitution and FC Art. 1 that marriage is an inviolable social institution. Courts therefore presume a marriage valid and require strong evidence to overturn it.

stem: A and B lived together openly for thirty years. They were known in their community as husband and wife, and the birth certificates of their children named them as married. No marriage certificate can be found. After B died, B's collateral relatives claimed that A is not B's surviving spouse. Which statement is correct?
choices: A must produce the marriage certificate; without it, no marriage can be proved
A and B are presumed to have been validly married, but the relatives may overcome the presumption by competent evidence to the contrary
A and B are conclusively presumed to have been married, so no contrary evidence may be received
The marriage may be proved only by the testimony of the solemnizing officer
None of the above
explanation: Under Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa), a man and woman deporting themselves as husband and wife are disputably presumed to have entered into a lawful contract of marriage. Civil Code Art. 220 adds that every intendment of law leans toward the validity of marriage. The marriage certificate (FC Arts. 6, 22) is the best evidence of marriage but not the only evidence. Tolentino notes that the testimony of a party or of witnesses to the ceremony, open cohabitation, and the children's birth and baptismal records are competent proof (see also Vda. de Jacob v. CA, 1999). The presumption is disputable, not conclusive, so c is wrong, and a and d state requirements the law does not impose.

stem: After undergoing sex reassignment in a foreign country, Jose, who is now using the name of "Josie," married his partner Ador. Is the marriage valid?
choices: Yes, the marriage is valid for as long as it is valid in the place where it is celebrated following Article 17 of the Civil Code.
Yes, the marriage is valid if all the essential and formal elements of marriage under the Family Code are present.
No, the marriage is not valid because one essential element of marriage is absent.
No, the marriage is not valid but is voidable because "Josie" concealed her real identity.
explanation: FC Art. 2(1) requires that the contracting parties be 'a male and a female'. In Silverio v. Republic (G.R. No. 174689, Oct. 22, 2007), the Supreme Court held that no Philippine law allows the change of the entry of sex in the birth certificate by reason of sex reassignment surgery. Sex is determined at birth. Jose therefore remains legally male, the parties are of the same sex, and an essential requisite is absent, so the marriage is void (Art. 4, par. 1). D is wrong because this is an absence of an essential requisite, not fraud under Art. 46.

stem: In December 2000, Michael and Anna, after obtaining a valid marriage license, went to the Office of the Mayor of Urbano, Bulacan, to get married. The Mayor was not there, but the Mayor's secretary asked Michael and Anna and their witnesses to fill up and sign the required marriage contract forms. The secretary then told them to wait and went out to look for the Mayor who was attending a wedding in a neighboring municipality. When the secretary caught up with the Mayor at the wedding reception, she showed him the marriage contract forms and told him that the couple and their witnesses were waiting in his office. The Mayor forthwith signed all the copies of the marriage contract, gave them to the secretary who returned to the Mayor's office. She then gave copies of the marriage contract to the parties and told Michael and Anna that they were already married. Thereafter, the couple lived together as husband and wife, and had three (3) sons. Is the marriage of Michael and Anna valid, voidable, or void?
choices: Valid, because they had a valid marriage license and the Mayor signed the marriage contract.
Valid, because the absence of the Mayor is a mere irregularity in a formal requisite.
Void, because there was no marriage ceremony and no declaration of consent in the presence of the solemnizing officer.
Voidable, because their consent was obtained by mistake as to the solemnization.
explanation: Void. Art. 2(2) requires consent freely given IN THE PRESENCE of the solemnizing officer. Art. 3(3) requires a marriage ceremony with the personal appearance of the parties before the solemnizing officer and their personal declaration, before at least two witnesses of legal age, that they take each other as husband and wife (see also Art. 6). Here the mayor merely signed forms away from the parties. There was no ceremony and no declaration before him, so both an essential and a formal requisite are absent, and the marriage is void ab initio under Art. 4, par. 1. Signing the marriage contract is not a substitute: the certificate is only evidence of the marriage, not a requisite. The children are illegitimate (Art. 165).

stem: One of the parties was 17 years old at the time of solemnization of the marriage. The fact that one of them is less than 18, does it pertain to legal impediment or legal capacity?
choices: Legal impediment
Legal capacity
Both legal impediment and legal capacity
Neither; it pertains only to a formal requisite
explanation: Being below 18 is a matter of LEGAL CAPACITY (Arts. 2(1), 5), not a legal impediment. Art. 5 itself distinguishes the two: 'Any male or female of the age of eighteen years or upwards not under any of the impediments mentioned in Articles 37 and 38, may contract marriage.' Legal impediments refer to Arts. 37 and 38 (incestuous and public-policy marriages). The marriage of a 17-year-old is still void, but under Art. 35(1) for lack of capacity, not because of an impediment. (Uribe recitation, Aug. 30, 2018.)

stem: One of the parties was 17 years old at the time of solemnization of the marriage. Why is there a need to make a distinction between legal impediment v. capacity?
choices: Because legal impediment is relevant for the application of Arts. 37 and 38 (e.g., legitimation of a child born to underage parents who later marry, so long as they do not fall under Arts. 37 and 38)
Because lack of capacity makes a marriage voidable while legal impediment makes it valid
Because only legal impediments may be ratified by free cohabitation
Because there is no practical difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: Uribe's point is that 'legal impediment' (Arts. 37-38) has independent consequences. For example, under the rules on legitimation (Art. 177, as amended by R.A. 9858), a child conceived and born outside wedlock of parents who, at the time of conception, were not disqualified by any impediment to marry each other, or were disqualified only because either or both were below 18, may be legitimated by their subsequent valid marriage. Minority is a matter of capacity, not an impediment, so it does not bar legitimation, while an Art. 37-38 impediment does. Choices b and c are wrong (lack of capacity under Art. 35(1) makes the marriage void and it cannot be ratified), and d ignores the distinction.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Any male or female of the age of eighteen years or upwards not under any of the impediments mentioned in Articles 37 and 38 may contract marriage.
2. A marriage contracted by a party below eighteen years of age is merely voidable if the parents of such party gave their consent.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is the text of FC Art. 5, so it is true. No. 2 is false: under Art. 35(1), marriages contracted by any party below eighteen years of age are void 'even with the consent of parents or guardians'. Tolentino explains that 18 is the age of legal capacity for both sexes and that below it a party cannot give binding consent. R.A. 11596 (2021) now also declares child marriages void ab initio and penalizes those who facilitate or solemnize them. Parental consent matters only for parties 18 to below 21 (Art. 14); without it, the marriage is voidable (Art. 45(1)).

stem: In 2025, A, a 17-year-old girl, was the offended party in a crime of seduction committed by B, 25. To extinguish B's criminal liability, A's parents consented to A's marriage to B, which was solemnized by a judge after a marriage license was somehow issued. The marriage is:
choices: Valid, because the marriage of the offender with the offended party is an exception recognized by the Revised Penal Code
Void, and the persons who facilitated or solemnized it may be held criminally liable under R.A. 11596
Voidable, because A was below 18 but her parents consented
Valid, but B remains criminally liable
None of the above
explanation: Under FC Arts. 5 and 35(1), a marriage contracted by a party below 18 is void even with parental consent. Tolentino (PDF p. 150, book p. 239) submitted that a girl below eighteen who was the victim of rape, seduction, abduction or acts of lasciviousness can validly marry the offender, treating such marriages as exceptional. That view is outdated: Art. 35(1) declares void marriages of parties below 18 even with parental consent, and R.A. 11596 declares child marriages void ab initio and penalizes those who facilitate or solemnize them. (R.A. 8353 also limits the pardon-by-marriage rule in rape.) Art. 344 of the Revised Penal Code (extinction of criminal liability by marriage of the offender to the offended party) presupposes a VALID marriage. It cannot validate a marriage that the Family Code and R.A. 11596 declare void.

stem: A and B were married in September 2, 1988 when both were only 17 years old. The marriage is:
choices: Valid if with the consent of their parents.
Voidable if without parental consent
voidable if without parental advice
Void even if with parental consent
Valid if both misrepresented as to their age
explanation: The Family Code took effect on August 3, 1988, so a marriage on September 2, 1988 is governed by it. Under Arts. 2(1) and 5, the minimum age of capacity is 18 for both parties. Under Art. 35(1), a marriage contracted by any party below 18 is void 'even with the consent of parents or guardians'. Parental consent (Art. 14) and advice (Art. 15) matter only for parties 18-21 and 21-25. Misrepresentation as to age cannot supply capacity the law withholds. R.A. 11596 (2021) now also penalizes child marriages.

stem: A marriage certificate is one of the formal requisites of marriage.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 3 enumerates only three formal requisites: (1) authority of the solemnizing officer; (2) a valid marriage license, except in the cases in Chapter 2; and (3) a marriage ceremony with the personal appearance of the parties before the solemnizing officer and their personal declaration, in the presence of at least two witnesses of legal age, that they take each other as husband and wife. The marriage certificate (also called the marriage contract) is not among them. It is merely the best evidence of the marriage (Arts. 6, 22-23), and failure to sign or register it does not affect validity. (Variants of this item say 'marriage contract' or 'formal contract'; the answer is the same.)

stem: The absence of any of the formal requisites of marriage shall render the marriage void ab initio.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 4, par. 1: 'The absence of any of the essential or formal requisites shall render the marriage void ab initio, EXCEPT as stated in Article 35(2).' Under Art. 35(2), a marriage solemnized by a person without authority is not void if either or both parties believed in good faith that the officer had authority. Also, the license requirement (a formal requisite) does not apply to the marriages of exceptional character in Arts. 27-34 (Art. 35(3)). Because of these exceptions the statement is not absolutely true. (Variants read 'essential or formal requisites' or 'essential and formal requisites'; they are false for the same reason.)

stem: The absence of any of the essential requisites shall render the marriage void ab initio.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Arts. 2 and 4, par. 1. The only exception in Art. 4, par. 1 (Art. 35(2), good-faith belief in the authority of the solemnizing officer) concerns a FORMAL requisite. There is no exception for the absence of an ESSENTIAL requisite: no legal capacity (e.g., same sex, below 18) or no consent at all. Such a marriage is always void ab initio. Contrast a DEFECT in an essential requisite (e.g., vitiated consent), which makes it voidable under Art. 45 (Art. 4, par. 2).

stem: A defect in any of the essential requisites shall not affect the validity of the marriage.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 4, par. 2: 'A defect in any of the essential requisites shall render the marriage voidable as provided in Article 45.' Examples are lack of parental consent for a party 18-21, insanity, fraud, force, intimidation or undue influence. The statement confuses this with Art. 4, par. 3, under which it is an IRREGULARITY in the FORMAL requisites that does not affect validity.

stem: An irregularity in the formal requisites shall:
choices: render the marriage void
render the marriage voidable
not affect the validity of the marriage
give rise to its correction
explanation: FC Art. 4, par. 3: 'An irregularity in the formal requisites shall not affect the validity of the marriage but the party or parties responsible for the irregularity shall be civilly, criminally and administratively liable.' It does not make the marriage void (that is for ABSENCE of a requisite, Art. 4, par. 1) or voidable (that is for a DEFECT in an ESSENTIAL requisite, Art. 4, par. 2). Examples include license issued in the wrong city, before the posting period ends, or without parental advice, and a judge solemnizing outside his territory.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The absence of any of the formal requisites shall render the marriage void ab initio.
2. No license shall be necessary for the marriage of a man and a woman who have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years and without any legal impediment to marry each other.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false: Art. 4, par. 1 states the rule 'except as stated in Article 35(2)' (good-faith belief in the authority of the solemnizing officer), and license-exempt marriages under Arts. 27-34 do not need the license. No. 2 is true: it is the first sentence of Art. 34. Under Niñal v. Bayadog and Manzano v. Sanchez, the five-year cohabitation must be exclusive, continuous and free of legal impediment, and there must be no impediment at the time of the marriage.

stem: The marriage will not be void even if:
choices: there is no certificate of legal capacity to contract marriage of an alien who is one of the contracting parties.
there was no parental consent and one of the contracting parties was 20 years old at the time of the solemnization of the marriage.
the marriage was solemnized outside the jurisdiction of the court.
all of the above
none of the above.
explanation: All three situations leave the marriage not void. (a) The certificate of legal capacity (Art. 21) is a requirement for issuing the license. Its absence is an irregularity in a formal requisite, and the alien's actual capacity is governed by his national law. (b) A party aged 18 to below 21 who marries without parental consent makes the marriage VOIDABLE, not void (Arts. 14, 45(1)). (c) A judge solemnizing outside his court's territorial jurisdiction commits only an irregularity in the formal requisite of authority (Navarro v. Domagtoy, 1996; Aranes v. Occiano, 2002). The marriage is valid but the judge is administratively liable.

stem: Which of the following will render a marriage VOID?
choices: The marriage was solemnized by a person not legally authorized to solemnize marriages, and both parties knew of his lack of authority
The marriage license was issued before the expiration of the ten-day period of posting of the notice of the application
The marriage was solemnized by a judge in a restaurant without a written request of the parties
The marriage license was issued by the local civil registrar without requiring the documentary proofs required by law
None of the above
explanation: Under FC Arts. 4 and 35(2), the ABSENCE of authority of the solemnizing officer makes the marriage void unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority. Since both parties knew he had none, the exception does not apply and the marriage is void. The others are mere irregularities in formal requisites that do not affect validity (Art. 4, par. 3): (b) early issuance of the license before the 10-day posting (Art. 17), (c) solemnization in a place other than those in Art. 8 without a written request, and (d) issuance without the documents required by Arts. 11-13. Tolentino (book p. 237) gives these as examples of irregularities.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A marriage which preceded the issuance of the marriage license is void, and the subsequent issuance of such license cannot render it valid.

2. The person solemnizing a marriage has the duty to investigate whether the license was issued by the local civil registrar of the habitual residence of either party; his failure to do so renders the marriage voidable.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true. A valid license is a formal requisite (Art. 3(2)), and a marriage without it is void (Arts. 4, 35(3)). A license issued after the ceremony cannot retroactively validate the marriage (Tolentino, book p. 235). No. 2 is false. The law imposes no duty on the solemnizing officer to investigate whether the license was issued by the registrar of the habitual residence of either party (Art. 9). He may presume regularity, and issuance by the wrong registrar is only an irregularity that does not affect validity, so it cannot make the marriage voidable. Voidability arises only from the defects in Art. 45.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. No prescribed form or religious rite for the solemnization of the marriage is required.
2. Marriage by proxy is valid in this jurisdiction, provided the proxy appears before the solemnizing officer in the presence of not less than two witnesses of legal age.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it is the first sentence of FC Art. 6. No. 2 is false. Art. 6 requires the contracting parties to 'appear personally before the solemnizing officer and declare in the presence of not less than two witnesses of legal age that they take each other as husband and wife' (see also Arts. 2(2), 3(3)). Tolentino (book pp. 240-241) concludes that a marriage by proxy is not legally possible in the Philippines. A proxy marriage celebrated ABROAD is a different question, governed by Art. 26, par. 1 (lex loci celebrationis).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The failure of the contracting parties to sign the marriage certificate renders the marriage void for want of a formal requisite.

2. In case of a marriage in articulo mortis, when the party at the point of death is unable to sign the marriage certificate, it shall be sufficient for one of the witnesses to the marriage to write the name of said party, which fact shall be attested by the solemnizing officer.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Signing the marriage certificate is not a requisite of marriage. Validity depends on the parties' personal appearance and declaration before the solemnizing officer and two witnesses (Arts. 2(2), 3(3), 6), and the certificate is only evidence. Tolentino (book pp. 241-242) treats non-signing, and even non-execution, of the certificate as at most an irregularity. No. 2 is true: it is Art. 6, par. 2 verbatim. In a marriage in articulo mortis, if the dying party cannot sign, one of the WITNESSES writes the party's name, and the solemnizing officer attests to this fact.

stem: Marriages may be solemnized by, except:
choices: Provincial Governor, within the province;
Any priest, rabbi, imam, or minister of any church or religious sect;
Any consul or vice-consul in the case provided in Article 10.
Any incumbent member of the judiciary within the court's jurisdiction
None of the above

stem: As of August 2, 1988, the following have the authority to solemnize marriage except:
choices: priest
incumbent member of the judiciary
imam
city mayor
none of the above
explanation: August 2, 1988 is one day BEFORE the Family Code took effect (August 3, 1988), so the Civil Code governed. Civil Code Art. 56 authorized justices and judges, priests and ministers of any denomination, and mayors of cities and municipalities to solemnize marriages. Imams could solemnize Muslim marriages under P.D. 1083 (1977). All four therefore had authority, so the answer is 'none of the above'. Compare the 1989 version of this item: from August 3, 1988 until the LGC of 1991, mayors had no authority.

choices: Priest
Incumbent member of the judiciary
Imam
City mayor
None of the above
explanation: On August 2, 1989 the Family Code was in force. Art. 7 as originally enacted dropped mayors from the list of solemnizing officers (Tolentino, book p. 242). Their authority was restored only by the Local Government Code of 1991 (R.A. 7160, effective January 1, 1992; Secs. 444(b)(1)(xviii) and 455(b)(1)(xviii)). stem: On July 30, 1988, Alex and Ben, both residents of Marikina, eloped and applied for a marriage license at the Manila City Hall. Alex was then 17. On December 5, 1988, using the marriage license issued by the civil registrar of Manila, Alex and Ben were married in Taguig by the city mayor of Makati. The only persons present were C and D, both 16 years old. Alex and Ben did not sign any marriage certificate. Assume that Alex had turned 18 (but was below 21) by December 5, 1988, that no parent ever consented, and that both Alex and Ben believed in good faith that the mayor had authority to marry them. The marriage is:
choices: Void, because city mayors had no authority to solemnize marriages at that time
Void, because the two witnesses were below the age of majority
Voidable, because Alex married without parental consent
Valid, because all the defects are mere irregularities in the formal requisites
Void, because the license was not issued by the civil registrar of the place where either party habitually resides
explanation: Age is reckoned at the time of solemnization, not of the license application (DOJ Opinion No. 146, s. 1991), so Alex had capacity on December 5, 1988. Being 18-21 and having eloped, however, Alex lacked parental consent, which makes the marriage voidable (Arts. 14, 45(1)). From August 3, 1988 until the LGC of 1991, mayors had no authority to solemnize marriages. The marriage would therefore be void under Art. 35(2), except that both parties believed in good faith that the mayor had authority. The minor witnesses, the license from Manila where neither party resides (Art. 9), and the unsigned certificate are mere irregularities (Art. 4, par. 3; Uribe counts only three formal requisites). The only remaining defect is in an essential requisite, so the marriage is voidable.
key_note: Converted from a class recitation that had no single answer. Uribe stressed that the result depends on Alex's age at solemnization and on the parties' good faith. Without good faith the marriage is void (Art. 35(2)). If Alex were still 17 on Dec. 5, 1988 it is void (Art. 35(1)). When grounds for both nullity and annulment exist, treat the marriage as void.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A marriage solemnized in Makati City by Mayor of San Juan is void.
2. A marriage is void if solemnized by one without authority to solemnize marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Mayors' authority to solemnize marriages comes from the LGC (Secs. 444(b)(1)(xviii), 455(b)(1)(xviii)). The samplex key reasons, by analogy with judges (Navarro v. Domagtoy), that a mayor solemnizing outside his territory commits at most an irregularity that does not affect validity, so the marriage is not void. Even on the stricter view that the mayor lacks authority outside his territory, the marriage would still not be void if either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority (Art. 35(2)), so No. 1 is not absolutely true either way. No. 2 is false because of the same Art. 35(2) exception: a marriage solemnized by one without authority is not void if either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority.
key_note: No Supreme Court case squarely rules on a mayor solemnizing outside his territory; the 'mere irregularity' reasoning is the samplex key's analogy to Navarro v. Domagtoy. Some commentators treat it as lack of authority. Either way No. 1 is false (good-faith exception), so the answer is unchanged.

explanation: No. 1 is false. In Navarro v. Domagtoy (1996) and Aranes v. Occiano (2002), the Court held that a judge who solemnizes a marriage outside his court's territorial jurisdiction commits an IRREGULARITY in a formal requisite (Art. 4, par. 3). Jurisdiction is not the same as authority. The marriage is valid, and only the judge is administratively liable. No. 2 is false because Art. 14 provides no suspension for lack of parental consent: the parties must simply exhibit the consent, and if they marry without it the marriage is voidable (Art. 45(1)). The three-month suspension applies to lack of parental ADVICE (Art. 15) and to a missing marriage-counseling certificate (Art. 16). (Standalone T/F versions, 'may suspend' or 'is void', are false for the same reasons.)
key_note: Some answer keys reasoned that No. 1 is false because of the Art. 35(2) good-faith exception. The correct reason is that solemnizing outside the judge's territory is a mere irregularity (Navarro v. Domagtoy), not a lack of authority.

stem: A marriage solemnized by a Presbyterian Minister where both parties are Catholics is valid; there is only an irregularity in a formal requisite.
choices: True
False
explanation: This is Uribe's recitation answer. The officer is an authorized minister, but Art. 7(2) adds the proviso 'that at least one of the contracting parties belongs to the solemnizing officer's church or religious sect'. Uribe treats non-compliance with this proviso as only an irregularity in the formal requisite of authority, so the marriage stays valid (Art. 4, par. 3) and the minister is liable.
key_note: Debatable. Under the contrary view (2006 Bar suggested answer; several commentators), the membership proviso limits the minister's authority. A marriage of two non-members would then be void under Art. 35(2) unless a party believed in good faith that he had authority, and some say a belief based on a mistake of law does not qualify. For Uribe's quizzes, follow his answer: valid, mere irregularity.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. For a priest, rabbi, imam or minister to solemnize a marriage, at least one of the contracting parties must belong to the solemnizing officer's church or religious sect.
2. For a priest or minister to validly solemnize a marriage, it is sufficient that he be registered with the local civil registrar of the place where the marriage is celebrated.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: FC Art. 7(2) authorizes a priest, rabbi, imam or minister who is (a) duly authorized by his church or religious sect, (b) registered with the civil registrar GENERAL, and (c) acting within the limits of the written authority granted by his church. It adds the proviso that at least one of the contracting parties belongs to his church or sect (Tolentino, book p. 243). No. 1 restates the proviso, so it is true (the proviso applies only to religious solemnizing officers, not to judges, consuls, etc.). No. 2 is false: registration is with the Civil Registrar General, not the local civil registrar, and registration alone is not enough.

stem: Which of the following has NO authority to solemnize the marriage described?
choices: The Philippine Consul-General in Dubai, for a marriage between two Filipinos
A ship captain, for a marriage in articulo mortis between passengers during a stopover at a port of call
A military commander of a unit who is a commissioned officer, in the absence of a chaplain, for a marriage in articulo mortis between civilians within the zone of military operation
The Philippine Ambassador to Japan, as head of the diplomatic mission, for a marriage between two Filipinos in Tokyo
None of the above
explanation: FC Arts. 7(5) and 10 grant authority to a consul-general, consul or vice-consul for marriages between Filipino citizens abroad. Tolentino (book p. 243) notes that an ambassador, though head of the diplomatic mission, has no such authority, because consuls handle matters affecting Filipino citizens. The others are authorized. (a) The consul-general may marry two Filipinos abroad. (b) Under Art. 31, a ship captain may solemnize an articulo mortis marriage between passengers or crew members while at sea or during stopovers at ports of call. (c) Under Art. 32, a military commander who is a commissioned officer may solemnize an articulo mortis marriage between persons within the zone of military operation, whether members of the armed forces or civilians, in the absence of the chaplain (Art. 7(4)).

stem: The First Officer of an airplane (not the airplane chief/pilot) has authority to solemnize a marriage in articulo mortis on board.
choices: True
False
explanation: Art. 7(3) authorizes 'any ship captain or airplane chief only in the case mentioned in Article 31' (Art. 31 says 'airplane pilot'). Uribe's answer is that a First Officer, not being the airplane chief, has no authority under Art. 7. A marriage he solemnizes is void for lack of authority unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority (Art. 35(2)). Uribe acknowledged the textual inconsistency between 'chief' in Art. 7 and 'pilot' in Art. 31.
key_note: The 1995 Bar suggested answer (hijacking problem) treated an assistant pilot acting for a chief pilot held hostage as authorized because of extraordinary circumstances. That reasoning is debatable and does not apply in ordinary situations.

stem: If the parties were married by the airplane chief in Manila Hotel (not on board the plane in flight), the marriage would be valid.
choices: True
False
explanation: An airplane chief's authority is special and limited. Under Arts. 7(3) and 31, he may solemnize only a marriage in articulo mortis between passengers or crew members, while the plane is in flight or during stopovers at ports of call. Uribe: 'only in flight' (technically, once the engine has started). A marriage he solemnizes in a hotel is solemnized by a person without authority. It is void unless either party believed in good faith that he had authority (Art. 35(2)), so the statement that it 'would be valid' is not absolutely true.

stem: Suppose the couple got married on September 1, 1994 at the Manila Hotel before the Philippine Consul General to Hongkong, who was on vacation in Manila. The couple executed an affidavit consenting to the celebration of the marriage at the Manila Hotel. Is the marriage valid?
choices: Valid, since the couple executed an affidavit consenting to the venue.
Valid, since consuls-general are authorized to solemnize marriages anywhere.
Void, since a consul has no authority to solemnize marriages in the Philippines – unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority.
Voidable.
explanation: Under Arts. 7(5) and 10, consuls-general, consuls and vice-consuls may solemnize marriages only 'between Filipino citizens abroad', in the consular office (Art. 8). They have no authority to solemnize marriages on Philippine soil, even while on vacation here. The affidavit on venue (Art. 8) cures only an irregularity of place. It cannot supply authority. The marriage is therefore void for lack of authority of the solemnizing officer (Art. 35(2)) unless either or both parties believed in good faith that he had authority.

stem: Agay, a Filipino citizen and Topacio, an Australian citizen, got married in the consular office of the Philippines in Australia. According to the laws of Australia, a marriage solemnized by a consular official is valid, provided that such marriage is celebrated in accordance with the laws of such consular official. Under Philippine law, what is the status of the marriage of Agay and Topacio? Choose the best answer.
choices: Void, because the consular official only has authority to solemnize marriages between Filipinos.
Valid, because according to the laws of Australia, such consular official has authority to celebrate the marriage.
Voidable, because there is an irregularity in the authority of the consular official to solemnize marriages.
Valid, because such marriage is recognized as valid in the place where it was celebrated.
explanation: Under FC Arts. 7(5) and 10, a Philippine consul may solemnize only marriages 'between Filipino citizens abroad'. Topacio is Australian, so the consul had no authority to marry him to Agay. Australian law itself makes the validity of a consular marriage depend on the consul's own (Philippine) law, so lex loci (Art. 26, par. 1) gives no independent basis of validity. The marriage is void for lack of authority (Arts. 4, 35(2)). On the given choices, the good-faith exception is not in issue. C is wrong because absence of authority is not a mere irregularity and is never a ground for annulment.

stem: Two college sweethearts were married inside a Roman Catholic church in the Philippines with a Supreme Court Justice serving as solemnizing officer. A few years following the ceremony, one of the two (2) filed an action for the declaration of nullity of marriage on the ground that the marriage was void ab initio because it was solemnized inside a Roman Catholic church by a Supreme Court Justice, and not by a Roman Catholic priest. Is the position legally tenable?
choices: Yes, because a marriage in a Catholic church may be solemnized only by a Catholic priest.
No, because a Supreme Court Justice has authority to solemnize marriages anywhere in the Philippines, and the venue is neither an essential nor a formal requisite.
Yes, because a member of the judiciary may solemnize marriages only in chambers or in open court.
No, but the marriage is voidable for irregularity in the venue.
explanation: Any incumbent member of the judiciary may solemnize marriages 'within the court's jurisdiction' (Art. 7(1)), and a Justice of the Supreme Court has jurisdiction over the entire Philippines. Art. 8 requires a judge to solemnize marriages in chambers or in open court, while churches, chapels and temples are the venues for religious solemnizing officers. But the place of the marriage is neither an essential nor a formal requisite (Arts. 2-3). A wrong venue is at most an irregularity that does not affect validity (Art. 4, par. 3). The marriage is valid and the action will fail.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Marriages contracted at the point of death and marriages in remote places in accordance with Article 29 may be solemnized elsewhere than in the chambers of the judge, in open court, in a church, chapel or temple, or in the consular office.
2. A marriage may be solemnized at a house or place designated in a sworn statement if either of the contracting parties requests the solemnizing officer in writing.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: FC Art. 8 requires public solemnization in the judge's chambers or open court, in the church, chapel or temple, or in the consular office, 'and not elsewhere, except in cases of marriages contracted at the point of death or in remote places in accordance with Article 29 of this Code, or where BOTH of the parties request the solemnizing officer in writing'. No. 1 is true. No. 2 is false because the written request must come from both parties, not either. In any case, solemnization in an unauthorized place is only an irregularity (Art. 4, par. 3).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A marriage certificate is one of the formal requisites of marriage.
2. A marriage license shall be issued by the local civil registrar of the city or municipality where both contracting parties habitually reside.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 3 lists only three formal requisites: authority of the solemnizing officer, a valid marriage license, and a marriage ceremony. The marriage certificate is merely evidence of the marriage (Arts. 6, 22). No. 2 is false: under Art. 9, the license is issued by the local civil registrar of the city or municipality where EITHER contracting party habitually resides, not both. Even a license issued by the registrar of a place where neither party resides is only an irregularity (Art. 4, par. 3). (A standalone T/F version of No. 2 appears in several samplexes; answer: False.)

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. In marriages between Filipino citizens abroad solemnized by a consul-general, consul or vice-consul, the issuance of the marriage license and the duties of the local civil registrar shall be performed by said consular official.

2. A marriage license shall be issued by the local civil registrar of the city or municipality where either contracting party habitually resides; a license obtained from the civil registrar of another place renders the marriage void.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it restates FC Art. 10, under which the consular official also performs the duties of the solemnizing officer. No. 2 is false. Its first clause is Art. 9, but obtaining the license from the registrar of a place where neither party resides is only an irregularity in a formal requisite (Art. 4, par. 3). The license still exists, so the marriage is valid. Tolentino (book pp. 244-245) adds that the solemnizing officer need not investigate where the license was issued.

stem: A marriage license is required in the following:
choices: A marriage in articulo mortis between passengers or crew members of airlines
A marriage in articulo mortis between persons within the zone of military operation
A marriage between Filipino citizens abroad solemnized by a consul
A marriage where the residence of either party is so located that there is no means of transportation to enable such party to appear personally before the local civil registrar
None of the above
explanation: Under Art. 10, in a marriage between Filipino citizens abroad solemnized by a consul, 'the issuance of the marriage license and the duties of the local civil registrar' are performed by the consular official. A license is therefore still required, and the consul issues it. The others are marriages of exceptional character exempt from the license requirement: (a) articulo mortis between passengers or crew members (Arts. 27, 31); (b) articulo mortis within the zone of military operation (Arts. 27, 32); and (d) residence with no means of transportation to appear before the LCR (Art. 28).
key_note: One samplex variant (Midterm) offers 'A marriage between Filipino citizens abroad' (without 'solemnized by a consul') alongside ethnic-community marriages (Art. 33). The keyed answer is the same, on the Art. 10 reasoning.

a marriage in articulo mortis between persons within the zone of military operations
a marriage where the residence of either party is so located that there is no means of transportation to enable such party to appear personally before the local civil registrar

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Where a marriage license is required, each of the contracting parties shall file separately a sworn application for such license with the proper local civil registrar.
2. The applicants, their parents or guardians shall be required to exhibit their residence certificates in connection with the securing of the marriage license.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it is the opening clause of FC Art. 11. The application must state, among others, full name, place of birth, age and date of birth, civil status, how and when any previous marriage was dissolved or annulled, present residence and citizenship, degree of relationship of the parties, and the parents' names. No. 2 is false: the last paragraph of Art. 11 says the applicants, their parents or guardians 'shall NOT be required to exhibit their residence certificates in any formality in connection with the securing of the marriage license.'

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A contracting party may furnish, in lieu of his birth or baptismal certificate, an instrument sworn to by two witnesses of lawful age, if the certificate has not yet been received although it was required of the person having custody thereof at least thirty days prior to the date of the application.

2. The presentation of the birth or baptismal certificate shall not be required when the local civil registrar shall, by merely looking at the applicants upon their personally appearing before him, be convinced that either or both of them have the required age.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Under FC Art. 12, par. 2, the substitute proof may be used if the certificate has not been received although it was required of its custodian 'at least FIFTEEN days prior to the date of the application'. The substitute is the current residence certificate or a sworn instrument containing the declaration of two witnesses of lawful age, with nearest of kin preferred. No. 2 is true: it is the last clause of Art. 12. The certificate is also dispensed with if the parents appear personally and swear to the correctness of the parties' lawful age.

stem: A, a widower, applies for a marriage license to marry B. A cannot secure the death certificate of his deceased wife. What must A do?
choices: Make an affidavit setting forth this circumstance, his actual civil status, and the name and date of death of his deceased spouse
Obtain a judicial declaration of presumptive death of his deceased wife
Present only his birth certificate, since his first marriage has been dissolved by death
Wait until the lapse of four years from the death of his wife
None of the above
explanation: FC Art. 13: a previously married applicant must furnish, INSTEAD of the birth or baptismal certificate, the death certificate of the deceased spouse or the judicial decree of absolute divorce, annulment or declaration of nullity of the previous marriage. 'In case the death certificate cannot be secured, the party shall make an affidavit setting forth this circumstance and his or her actual civil status and the name and date of death of the deceased spouse.' A declaration of presumptive death (Art. 41) is for an ABSENT spouse whose death is uncertain, not one known to be dead.

stem: Any contracting party between the age of twenty-one and twenty-five shall be obliged to ask their parents or guardian for consent upon the intended marriage.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 15 requires parties between 21 and 25 to ask their parents or guardian for ADVICE, not consent. Parental CONSENT is required only of parties between 18 and 21 not emancipated by a previous marriage (Art. 14). Lack of consent makes the marriage voidable (Art. 45(1)). Lack of advice only delays issuance of the license for three months and does not affect validity.

stem: Any contracting party between the age of 21 and 25 shall be obliged to ask their parents or guardian for advice upon the intended marriage
choices: True
False
explanation: This is the first sentence of FC Art. 15. If advice is not obtained, or is unfavorable, the license shall not be issued until three months after the completion of the publication of the application. A sworn statement that advice was sought, together with the written advice if any, must be attached to the application, and the parents' refusal to give advice must be stated in it. Compare the 'consent' version of this item, which is false.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The parental consent required of contracting parties between eighteen and twenty-one shall be manifested in writing by the interested party, who personally appears before the proper local civil registrar, or in the form of an affidavit made in the presence of two witnesses and attested before any official authorized by law to administer oaths.

2. The consent to the marriage of a contracting party between eighteen and twenty-one may be given by the father, mother, surviving parent or guardian, or persons having legal charge of the party, in any order.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it reproduces the second sentence of FC Art. 14. The personal manifestation is recorded in both applications, and the affidavit, if executed instead, is attached to them. No. 2 is false: Art. 14 requires the consent of the 'father, mother, surviving parent or guardian, or persons having legal charge of them, IN THE ORDER MENTIONED' (see also Art. 45(1), 'in that order'). Tolentino notes that the consent should refer to the marriage with the particular person intended, not a blanket authorization.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A person between eighteen and twenty-one years of age whose previous marriage was terminated by the death of the spouse must again secure parental consent before contracting a subsequent marriage.
2. The reduction of the age of majority to eighteen by R.A. No. 6809 did not dispense with the requirement of parental consent for contracting parties between eighteen and twenty-one.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 14 applies to parties between 18 and 21 'NOT having been emancipated by a previous marriage'. Tolentino (book pp. 248-249) explains that a person below 21 whose earlier marriage ended with the spouse's death does not need parental consent to remarry, because consent was given in the first marriage and need not be repeated. No. 2 is true. R.A. 6809 (1989) lowered the age of majority to 18 but expressly provides that 'contracting marriage shall require parental consent until the age of twenty-one'.

stem: A, 22 years old, and B, 20 years old, applied for a marriage license on January 2, 2011. Without parental consent or advice, the civil registrar issued the license on January 15, 2011. They were married on May 5, 2011. Is the marriage valid?
choices: Valid, because all the essential and formal requisites are present without any defect in the former or any irregularity in the latter.
Voidable, because one of the contracting parties is below 21 and there was no parental consent.
Void, because the license had already expired
Valid, but there was an irregularity in the issuance of a marriage license.
explanation: B, 20 and never married, needed parental consent (Art. 14). Marrying without it makes the marriage VOIDABLE under Art. 45(1), ratifiable by free cohabitation after B turns 21. The license was not expired: issued January 15, it was valid for 120 days (Art. 20), until about May 15, so the May 5 marriage was within the period. Issuing the license without A's parental advice (A is 22; Art. 15) and without the counseling certificate (Art. 16) before three months had passed are irregularities that do not affect validity. Because of the defect in B's consent, however, 'valid but irregular' is not the answer.
key_note: Note: the samplex key marked 'Valid, but there was an irregularity in the issuance of the marriage license'; this is incorrect because B, 20 and not emancipated by a previous marriage, married without parental consent, which makes the marriage voidable (Art. 45(1)). That key fits only the version where B is a widow. (A variant with the license issued Jan. 5 and the marriage on May 1 has the same answer.)

stem: A, 22 years old, and B, a widow, 20 years old, applied for a marriage license on January 2, 2011. Without parental consent nor advice, the civil registrar issued a license on January 15, 2011. They were married on May 5, 2011. Is the marriage valid?
choices: Valid, because all the essential and formal requisites are present without any defect in the former nor any irregularity in the latter.
Voidable, because one of the contracting parties is below 21 and there was no parental consent.
Void, because the license had already expired.
Valid, but there was an irregularity in the issuance of the marriage license.
explanation: B, though only 20, is a widow emancipated by a previous marriage, so she needs no parental consent (Art. 14). A, 22, needed parental advice (Art. 15) and marriage counseling (Art. 16). Without them the license should have been withheld until three months after publication, so issuing it on January 15 was an irregularity. It does not affect validity (Art. 4, par. 3; Art. 16, par. 1). The license, valid for 120 days from January 15 (Art. 20), had not expired on May 5. The marriage is valid, but the license was irregularly issued.

stem: What is the status of the following marriage and why? A marriage between two 19-year-olds without parental consent.
choices: Valid, but the parties are subject to administrative liability.
Voidable, for lack of parental consent of parties between 18 and 21.
Void, for lack of legal capacity.
Valid, since parties 18 and above have full capacity to marry.
explanation: Voidable. Parties aged 18 to below 21 have legal capacity (Art. 5) but must obtain parental consent (Art. 14), and R.A. 6809 retained this requirement. A marriage solemnized without it may be annulled under Art. 45(1). Under Art. 47(1), the action may be brought by the party concerned within five years after reaching 21, or by the parent or guardian at any time before the party reaches 21. It is ratified if the party, after reaching 21, freely cohabits with the other as husband and wife. It is not void because the parties are not below 18 (Art. 35(1)).

stem: If one of the contracting parties was 19 years old at the time of the application for a marriage license and he did not present parental consent, the local civil registrar can refuse to issue the license.
choices: True
False
explanation: This is Uribe's recitation answer. The registrar's duty to issue the license is ministerial. Under Art. 18, even when an impediment is known to him, he only notes its particulars and his findings in the application and 'shall nonetheless issue said license after the completion of the period of publication, unless ordered otherwise by a competent court'. Lack of parental consent does not make the marriage void; it only makes it voidable (Art. 45(1)). A party who was previously married would not need consent at all (Art. 14).
key_note: Debatable. Contrary view: Art. 14 requires parties 18-21 to 'exhibit' the parental consent 'in addition to the requirements of the preceding articles', and Art. 18 speaks only of impediments. On that reading, the registrar may withhold the license until the consent is presented. For Uribe's quizzes, follow his answer (False).

stem: Even if there is lack of parental advice, despite the fact that one of the contracting parties is between 18 and 21, there will be no irregularity in the issuance of the marriage license.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 15 requires parental ADVICE only of parties between 21 and 25. A party between 18 and 21 needs parental CONSENT instead (Art. 14), so the absence of 'advice' for that party is not a deficiency, and issuing the license on that account involves no irregularity. If consent is also lacking, the marriage is voidable (Art. 45(1)), but that is a different matter. Uribe's quizzes reward reading the age brackets exactly.
key_note: Uribe's key (CivRev 2025 Quiz 3 #3) is True: the item tests that advice (Art. 15) is not required of a party aged 18-21, who needs consent instead (Art. 14). Read it as 'the lack of advice of that party causes no irregularity'. If another party is 21-25 and lacks advice, or the license is otherwise irregular, that is a different defect not raised by the statement.

stem: There may not be an irregularity in the issuance of a marriage license even if:
choices: there is lack of parental advice
none of the contracting parties habitually resides in the city where the license was issued.
there is no certificate of legal capacity to contract marriage of an alien who is one of the contracting parties.
there is lack of publication of the application for a marriage license.
none of the above.
explanation: If parental advice is lacking (Art. 15), the license 'shall not be issued till after three months following the completion of the publication'. Lack of advice only suspends issuance. A license issued after the three months, even without advice, is regularly issued, so lack of advice need not involve any irregularity. Each of the others is necessarily an irregularity: (b) issuance by the registrar of a place where neither party habitually resides (Art. 9); (c) no certificate of legal capacity for an alien party (Art. 21); and (d) no publication of the application (Art. 17).

stem: What is the status of the following marriage and why? A marriage between two 21-year-olds without parental advice.
choices: Valid; lack of parental advice is a mere irregularity that does not affect validity.
Voidable, at the instance of the parents.
Void, for absence of a formal requisite.
Void, because the license could not have been issued.
explanation: Valid. For parties between 21 and 25, the absence of parental advice only means the license may not be issued until three months after the completion of publication (Art. 15). If the license is issued after that, there is no irregularity at all. If it is issued earlier, the early issuance is an irregularity in the formal requisite of a license that does not affect validity, without prejudice to the liability of those responsible (Art. 4, par. 3). Lack of parental advice is not a ground for annulment (Art. 45(1) covers only lack of parental consent for parties 18 to below 21).

stem: X, 23 years old and Y, a widow, 20 years old, applied for a marriage license on January 2, 2019. Without parental consent nor advice, they were married on May 31, 2019. Is the marriage valid?
choices: May be valid, because all the essential and formal requisites are present and there may not be an irregularity in the issuance of the license.
Voidable, because one of the contracting parties is below 21 and there was no parental consent.
Valid, but there was an irregularity in the issuance of the marriage license
Void, because the license had already expired.
none of the above
explanation: Y, a widow, is emancipated by her previous marriage and needs no parental consent (Art. 14), so b is wrong. X, 23, needed parental advice. Without it, the license could issue only three months after publication was completed (Arts. 15, 16), roughly mid-April 2019 if posting started on January 2. The facts do not say when the license was issued. A license issued in April would be properly issued and still valid on May 31 (120 days, Art. 20), so expiry cannot be assumed. On these facts the marriage MAY be valid with no irregularity.
key_note: Note: the quiz key (class answer) marked d (expired license, assuming issuance around Jan. 15); this is incorrect because the issuance date is not given. Uribe himself answered a in the class discussion.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. In the cases where parental consent or parental advice is needed, the party or parties concerned shall attach a certificate that the contracting parties have undergone marriage counselling.
2. Should only one of the contracting parties need parental consent or parental advice, only that party is required to undergo the marriage counselling.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: FC Art. 16 requires the parties, where parental consent or advice is needed, to attach a certificate from a priest, imam or minister authorized under Art. 7, or an accredited marriage counselor, that they have undergone marriage counseling. No. 1 is true: it paraphrases Art. 16, par. 1. (Note that the need depends on whether consent or advice is actually required, not on age alone: a party 18-21 emancipated by a previous marriage needs no parental consent, Art. 14.) No. 2 is false: Art. 16, par. 2 provides that 'should only one of the contracting parties need parental consent or parental advice, the OTHER party must be present at the counseling.' Failure to attach the certificate suspends issuance of the license for three months from the completion of publication, but issuance within that period does not affect validity. It only subjects the issuing officer to administrative sanctions.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The issuance of the marriage license before the completion of the ten-day period of posting of the notice renders the marriage void for want of a valid license.

2. In case of any impediment known to the local civil registrar, he shall note down the particulars thereof and his findings thereon in the application, but shall nonetheless issue the license after the completion of the period of publication, unless ordered otherwise by a competent court.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Art. 17 requires the notice to be posted for ten consecutive days and the license to be issued after the period of publication. Issuing it before then is an irregularity in a formal requisite that does not invalidate the marriage (Art. 4, par. 3; Tolentino, book p. 254). No. 2 is true: it reproduces Art. 18. Unlike the old Civil Code, the registrar does not withhold the license because of a reported impediment. He notes it and must still issue the license unless a competent court orders otherwise. If the impediment really exists, the marriage is void on that ground, not because of the license.

stem: In case of any impediment known to the local civil registrar or brought to his attention, he shall not issue the marriage license, unless ordered otherwise by a competent court at his own instance or that of any interested party.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 18 states the opposite. The registrar 'shall note down the particulars thereof and his findings thereon in the application for marriage license, but shall NONETHELESS ISSUE said license after the completion of the period of publication, unless ordered otherwise by a competent court at his own instance or that of any interested party.' No filing fee is charged for the petition and no bond is required. Issuing the license is ministerial, and it is the court, not the registrar, that may stop it.

2. In case of any impediment known to the local registrar or brought to his attention, he shall nonetheless issue said license after the completion of the period of publication, unless otherwise ordered by a competent court at his own instance.

Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false

It is neither an essential nor a formal requisite, so its absence is at most an irregularity (Art. 4, par. 3). Whether the alien actually has capacity depends on his national law. No. 2 is false because it omits a phrase: under Art. 18, the court may order otherwise 'at his own instance OR THAT OF ANY INTERESTED PARTY.' The standalone T/F version of No. 2 is likewise false.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The marriage license shall be issued free of charge to indigent parties, that is, those who have no visible means of income or whose income is insufficient for their subsistence, a fact established by their affidavit or by their oath before the local civil registrar.
2. It shall be the duty of the local civil registrar to prepare the documents required for the marriage license and to administer oaths to all interested parties for a reasonable fee.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it reproduces the last sentence of FC Art. 19. Otherwise the registrar collects only the fees prescribed by law or regulations, and 'no other sum shall be collected in the nature of a fee or tax of any kind'. No. 2 is false: Art. 24 requires the local civil registrar to prepare the documents and administer oaths to all interested parties 'WITHOUT ANY CHARGE in both cases'. The documents and affidavits filed in connection with license applications are also exempt from documentary stamp tax.

stem: The license shall be valid in any part of the Philippines for a period of four months from the date of issue.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 20: 'The license shall be valid in any part of the Philippines for a period of one hundred twenty days from the date of issue, and shall be deemed automatically cancelled at the expiration of the said period if the contracting parties have not made use of it.' The expiry date is stamped in bold on the license. A month is 30 days (Civil Code Art. 13; Administrative Code of 1987, Sec. 31, unless a specific calendar month is meant), so four months equals 120 days. The '120 days' version of this item is also true.

stem: A and B obtained a marriage license issued on January 2, 2025 by the civil registrar of Lucena City. They were married in Manila on June 15, 2025 using that license. The marriage is:
choices: Void
Valid, but the solemnizing officer is administratively liable
Voidable
Valid, because a marriage license is valid in any part of the Philippines
None of the above
explanation: Under FC Art. 20, the license is valid anywhere in the Philippines for 120 days from issue and is 'deemed automatically cancelled' if not used. Counting from January 2, 2025, the 120 days ended on May 2, 2025. A marriage on June 15, 2025 was therefore solemnized without a license. This is the ABSENCE of a formal requisite, not a mere irregularity, so the marriage is void ab initio (Arts. 4, 35(3); Tolentino, book p. 256). Choice d misreads Art. 20: the license is valid anywhere in the Philippines only within the 120-day period.

stem: Stateless persons or refugees from other countries shall submit a certificate of legal capacity.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 21, par. 2: 'Stateless persons or refugees from other countries shall, IN LIEU OF the certificate of legal capacity herein required, submit an affidavit stating the circumstances showing such capacity to contract marriage.' Having no state, or being unable to get one from their own state, they cannot obtain a certificate from diplomatic or consular officials. Tolentino adds that their capacity is determined by Philippine law.

stem: The lack of certificate of legal capacity does not affect the validity of the marriage.
choices: True
False
explanation: The certificate of legal capacity (Art. 21) is a document required BEFORE a license can be obtained. It is neither an essential requisite (Art. 2) nor a formal requisite (Art. 3). Its absence is at most an irregularity in the issuance of the license, which does not affect validity (Art. 4, par. 3; DOJ Opinion No. 050, s. 1991). Whether the foreigner actually had capacity is a separate question governed by his national law. In Garcia v. Recio (2001), the Court treated a duly authenticated certificate as only prima facie evidence of capacity.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. When either or both of the contracting parties are citizens of a foreign country, it shall be necessary for them, before a marriage license can be obtained, to submit a certificate of legal capacity to contract marriage, issued by their respective diplomatic or consular officials.
2. Stateless persons or refugees from other countries shall, in lieu of the certificate of legal capacity, submit an affidavit stating the circumstances showing such capacity to contract marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: Both statements reproduce FC Art. 21, pars. 1 and 2. A foreigner's capacity to marry is governed by his national law (nationality principle). The certificate from his diplomatic or consular officials is the means of proving it before the license issues. A stateless person or refugee, who cannot obtain such a certificate, submits his own affidavit of the circumstances showing capacity, and his capacity is determined by Philippine law (Tolentino, book pp. 256-257). Absence of the certificate does not by itself affect validity.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The local civil registrar shall enter all applications for marriage licenses filed with him in a registry book strictly in the order in which the same are received.
2. The marriage certificate shall state, among others, that the parties have entered into a marriage settlement, if any, attaching a copy thereof.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: Both are true. No. 1 reproduces FC Art. 25. The registrar also records the names of the applicants, the date the license was issued and other necessary data. No. 2 reproduces Art. 22(7). The certificate, in which the parties declare that they take each other as husband and wife, must also state the parties' names, sex and age; citizenship, religion and habitual residence; the date and precise time of celebration; that the license was issued (except in license-exempt marriages); and compliance with parental consent and advice in appropriate cases.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. The marriage certificate is the best proof of marriage, but it is not the only proof; the testimony of one of the parties or of persons present at the celebration is competent proof of the marriage.
2. The failure of the solemnizing officer to send copies of the marriage certificate to the local civil registrar within fifteen days invalidates the marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true (Tolentino, book pp. 258-259; Rule 131, Sec. 3(aa); Civil Code Art. 220). No. 2 is false. Art. 23 does require the solemnizing officer to give the original certificate to either party and to send the duplicate and triplicate to the LCR of the place of solemnization 'not later than fifteen days after the marriage'. He keeps the quadruplicate, the original license and, in proper cases, the venue affidavit. But the certificate and its registration are not requisites of marriage, so non-compliance does not affect validity and only exposes the officer to liability.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. In marriages in articulo mortis or in remote places without means of transportation, the contracting parties shall state in an affidavit executed before the local civil registrar that the marriage was performed in articulo mortis or that the residence of either party is so located that there is no means of transportation.

2. The original of the affidavit required for marriages in articulo mortis or in remote places, together with a legible copy of the marriage contract, shall be sent by the person solemnizing the marriage to the local civil registrar of the municipality where it was performed within thirty days after the performance of the marriage.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Under FC Art. 29, the SOLEMNIZING OFFICER, not the parties, executes the affidavit before the LCR or any person authorized to administer oaths. It states that the marriage was performed in articulo mortis, or that the residence of either party (specifying the barrio or barangay) has no means of transportation, and that he took the necessary steps to ascertain the parties' ages and relationship and the absence of legal impediment. Compare Art. 34, where the PARTIES execute the affidavit of five-year cohabitation and the officer also states under oath that he found no legal impediment. No. 2 is true: it reproduces Art. 30.

stem: Which of the following periods is CORRECTLY stated?
choices: The notice of the application for a marriage license shall be posted for fifteen consecutive days.
The solemnizing officer shall send the duplicate and triplicate copies of the marriage certificate to the local civil registrar not later than thirty days after the marriage.

The affidavit of the solemnizing officer in a marriage in articulo mortis, together with a legible copy of the marriage contract, shall be sent to the local civil registrar within thirty days after the performance of the marriage.
Failure to attach the certificate of marriage counseling shall suspend the issuance of the marriage license for ninety days from the filing of the application.
None of the above
explanation: Only c is correct (Art. 30: within thirty days). (a) Art. 17 requires posting for TEN consecutive days. (b) Art. 23 requires sending the duplicate and triplicate copies not later than FIFTEEN days after the marriage. (d) Art. 16 suspends issuance for THREE MONTHS from the COMPLETION OF THE PUBLICATION, not from the filing of the application. Other periods to remember: the license is valid for 120 days (Art. 20), and a birth certificate must have been requested at least 15 days before the application to use substitute proof (Art. 12).

stem: All marriages solemnized outside the Philippines, in accordance with the laws in force in the country where they were solemnized, and valid there as such, shall also be valid in this country.
choices: True
False
explanation: FC Art. 26, par. 1 adopts lex loci celebrationis but adds 'EXCEPT those prohibited under Articles 35(1), (4), (5) and (6), 36, 37 and 38.' These are: a party below 18; bigamous or polygamous marriages not under Art. 41; mistake as to identity; subsequent marriages void under Art. 53; psychological incapacity; incestuous marriages; and marriages void for public policy. Such marriages are void here even if valid where celebrated. Because of these exceptions, the statement is not absolutely true.

stem: the marriage of A and B, both Filipinos, were solemnized in London in accordance with the laws in force in London and valid there as such. the marriage shall also be valid here in the Philippines even if:
choices: A and B are first cousins
B was only 17 during the marriage and there was no parental consent
C represented B during the marriage
bigamous marriage not falling under Article 41 of the Family Code
none of the above
explanation: Under Art. 26, par. 1, a marriage valid where celebrated is valid here, except those prohibited under Arts. 35(1), (4), (5), (6), 36, 37 and 38. A proxy marriage involves the FORM of celebration (personal appearance), which is governed by lex loci celebrationis and is not among the exceptions. If valid in London, it is valid here. The others are exceptions: (a) first cousins are collateral blood relatives within the fourth civil degree (Art. 38(1)); (b) a party below 18 (Art. 35(1)), void even with parental consent; (d) a bigamous marriage not falling under Art. 41 (Art. 35(4)).
key_note: Some commentators (e.g., Sempio-Diy) argue that personal appearance goes to consent, an essential requisite, so a proxy marriage of Filipinos abroad would be void despite lex loci. Uribe's key (and his recitation answer) follows lex loci: valid.

stem: The marriage of A and B, both Filipinos, were solemnized in London in accordance with the laws in force in London and valid there as such. The marriage shall also be valid here in the Philippines even if:
choices: A and B are first cousins.
B was only 17 during the marriage and there was no parental consent.
Bigamous marriage not falling under Article 41 of the Family Code.
There was mistake of one contracting party as to the identity of the other.
None of the above.
explanation: Each choice is an exception under Art. 26, par. 1, so the marriage would be void here despite its validity in London. (a) First cousins: Art. 38(1), collateral blood relatives up to the fourth civil degree. (b) A party aged 17: Art. 35(1), void whether or not parents consented. (c) A bigamous marriage not falling under Art. 41: Art. 35(4). (d) Mistake as to the identity of the other party: Art. 35(5). (Studocu variants read 'B was only 17 but there was parental consent'; the answer is the same.)

stem: The marriage of A and B, both Filipinos, were solemnized in London in accordance with the laws in force in London and valid there as such. The marriage may be valid under Philippine law even if:
choices: A is the first cousin of B.
B was only 17 during the marriage and there was no parental consent.
the marriage is bigamous
There was mistake of one contracting party as to the identity of the other
None of the above.
explanation: The stem asks what MAY leave the marriage valid. Art. 26, par. 1 excepts only bigamous marriages 'not falling under Article 41' (Art. 35(4)). A subsequent marriage contracted after a well-founded belief that the prior spouse is dead, under Art. 41, is valid. Since choice c says only 'the marriage is bigamous' without excluding Art. 41, the marriage may still be valid. The other choices are always void: (a) Art. 38(1); (b) Art. 35(1), below 18, with or without consent; (d) Art. 35(5).
key_note: The class consensus was e (all excluded by Art. 26(1)); Uribe agreed with c in the discussion because of the word 'may' and the Art. 41 carve-out. Read the exact wording: 'bigamous marriage NOT falling under Art. 41' (another version) is always void.

stem: The marriage of A and B, both Filipinos, were solemnized in London in accordance with the laws in force in London and valid there as such. The marriage shall be void here in the Philippines if:
choices: A was 18 years old, without parental authority.
It is a proxy marriage.
A & B are stepbrother and stepsister.
The marriage was solemnized by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
None of the above.
explanation: None of these is among the Art. 26, par. 1 exceptions. (a) A party aged 18 without parental consent ('authority' in the source) makes the marriage merely VOIDABLE (Art. 45(1)). Voidable marriages are not excepted, so it is valid until annulled. (b) A proxy marriage concerns form, governed by lex loci celebrationis. (c) Stepbrother and stepsister are not within the prohibited degrees. Art. 38(2) bars only step-parents and step-children, and the Family Code dropped the Civil Code's broader list. (d) The solemnizing officer's authority is a formal requisite, governed by the law of the place of celebration.
key_note: One Studocu copy marks b (proxy) in red, conflicting with its bold e. The answer is e: a proxy marriage valid where celebrated is valid here under Art. 26, par. 1.
