stem: The marriage of A and B, both Filipinos, were solemnized in London in accordance with the laws in force in London and valid there as such. The marriage shall be void here in the Philippines if:
choices: A was 18 years old, without parental authority.
It is a proxy marriage.
A and B are stepbrother and stepsister.
A and B are adopted children of the same adopter.
The marriage was solemnized by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.
explanation: A marriage between adopted children of the same adopter is void for reasons of public policy under Art. 38(8), which is one of the exceptions in Art. 26, par. 1. It is void here even if valid in London. The others do not make the marriage void. (a) A party aged 18 without parental consent: voidable only (Art. 45(1)). (b) A proxy marriage: form, governed by lex loci. (c) Step-siblings: not prohibited under Art. 38. (e) Solemnization by the Prime Minister: authority is a formal matter governed by lex loci.
key_note: Note: the samplex key marked b (proxy marriage); this is incorrect because the form of the ceremony, including a proxy marriage, is governed by lex loci celebrationis (Art. 26, par. 1). Art. 38(8) (adopted children of the same adopter) IS an Art. 26 exception. The compiler also flagged these answers as untrusted.

stem: A and B were supposed to be married in New York. However, a day before marriage, A was in California and he had to attend to a very important matter so he asked a brother to represent him in the marriage ceremony. The brother represented him, and there was a ceremony (A was not there). What is the status of the marriage?
choices: Valid if valid where celebrated (lex loci celebrationis, FC 26), even if A and B were Filipinos, unless it falls under the exceptions in FC 26
Void because a proxy marriage is always void
Voidable on the ground of mistake as to identity
Valid only if A and B were not Filipinos
explanation: Uribe's answer: a proxy marriage abroad is valid if valid where celebrated (lex loci celebrationis, Art. 26, par. 1), even if A and B are Filipinos. The exception is when the marriage falls under Arts. 35(1), (4), (5), (6), 36, 37 or 38. Personal appearance is a matter of form (Arts. 3(3), 6), and form is governed by the law of the place of celebration. A proxy marriage could not be validly celebrated IN the Philippines (Art. 6). C is wrong because the brother's appearance involves no mistake as to identity.
key_note: Debated: some authors (e.g., Sempio-Diy) treat personal appearance as part of consent, an essential requisite, so a proxy marriage of Filipinos abroad would be void. Uribe follows lex loci.

stem: A, a member of a popular boy band in the Philippines, got his girlfriend, B, pregnant. A and B got married in Hong Kong where the legal age to get married was at least 15 years old. At the time of their marriage, A and B were 17 and 16 years old, respectively, and were both Filipino citizens. Subsequently, A continued with his career while B hid her pregnancy in the United States of America. She only returned to the Philippines after she gave birth to their son. By then though, B was already tired of being A's deep dark secret. She thus filed a petition for declaration of nullity of marriage on the ground that her marriage with A is void. Will the petition prosper?
choices: No, because the marriage is valid in Hong Kong where it was celebrated and is thus valid here under Art. 26.
Yes, because their capacity is governed by Philippine law, and a marriage of a party below 18 is void, an exception to Art. 26(1).
No, because the marriage is merely voidable for lack of parental consent and has been ratified.
No, because B is in estoppel, having freely entered into the marriage.
explanation: Yes. Art. 26, par. 1 recognizes marriages valid where celebrated, but Art. 35(1) is an express exception. The legal capacity of Filipinos is governed by Philippine law even abroad (Civil Code Art. 15). A and B were 17 and 16, below the minimum age of 18, so the marriage is void ab initio even though Hong Kong allows marriage at 15. R.A. 11596 (2021) also declares child marriages void and imprescriptibly assailable. The action for nullity does not prescribe (Art. 39), and estoppel or ratification cannot validate a void marriage.

src: QuAMTO – 2003 Bar; Bar Q&A in PFR Reviewer 2013 (elmerpaquitolalong)
stem: Gene and Jane, Filipinos, met and got married in England while both were taking up postgraduate courses there. A few years after their graduation, they decided to annul their marriage. Jane filed an action to annul her marriage to Gene in England on the ground of the latter's sterility, a ground for annulment of marriage in England. The English court decreed the marriage annulled. Returning to the Philippines, Gene asked you whether or not he would now be free to marry his former girlfriend. What would your legal advice be?
choices: Yes, because the annulment was validly decreed in England where they were married.
Yes, provided the English decree is judicially recognized under Art. 26(2).
Yes, because sterility amounts to physical incapacity to consummate the marriage.
No, because as Filipinos their marriage may be annulled only on grounds under Philippine law, and sterility is not a ground under Art. 45.
explanation: No. The marriage was valid in form under English law (Art. 26, par. 1). Gene and Jane, however, remain Filipinos, and under Civil Code Art. 15 laws on family rights and duties and on status bind them even abroad. The annulment of their marriage must rest on a ground recognized by Philippine law. Sterility is not a ground under Art. 45, and it differs from physical incapacity to consummate (impotence) under Art. 45(5). The English decree therefore has no effect here, Gene remains married, and Art. 26(2) is irrelevant because neither spouse is an alien.
key_note: The bar reviewers note an alternative view: voidability is governed by lex loci celebrationis, so the English annulment would be valid. The main answer (No) follows the nationality principle.

stem: Under Article 26, paragraph 2 of the Family Code, the reckoning point is not the citizenship of the parties at the time of the celebration of the marriage, but their citizenship at the time a valid divorce is obtained abroad capacitating the alien to remarry.
choices: True
False
explanation: This is the holding of Republic v. Orbecido III (G.R. No. 154380, Oct. 5, 2005). Art. 26, par. 2 applies 'to include cases which involve parties who, at the time of the celebration of the marriage were Filipino citizens, but later on, one of them becomes naturalized as a foreign citizen and obtains a divorce decree.' The reckoning point is the parties' citizenship when the valid divorce is obtained abroad. Otherwise an absurd result follows: the alien spouse would be free to remarry while the Filipino spouse stays married to no one.

stem: A and B, both Filipinos, got married in Tacloban City in 1995. Thereafter, A went to New York to work as a nurse, where he met C, also a Filipino citizen. In 1998, A obtained a divorce decree in New York. He became a citizen of New York in 2001. In 2002, A married C. In 2003, B married D in Tacloban City. Is the marriage between B and D valid?
choices: Valid, because a divorce decree was obtained by A, thus, capacitating B to remarry.
Void, because A and B were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, therefore Article 26, par. 2 does not apply.
Valid, because when B married D, A was no longer a Filipino citizen.
Void, because A was still a Filipino at the time the divorce decree was obtained, thus, did not capacitate B to remarry D.
explanation: Under Republic v. Orbecido III (2005), Art. 26(2) is applied by looking at citizenship at the time the divorce is obtained. In 1998 A was still a Filipino. A divorce obtained by a Filipino married to another Filipino is not recognized here, because Civil Code Art. 15 binds Filipinos even abroad. His later naturalization in 2001 does not validate it retroactively. The A-B marriage subsisted, B had no capacity to remarry, and B's 2003 marriage to D is bigamous and void (Art. 35(4)). Choice b reaches the right result for the wrong reason (it uses citizenship at the time of celebration), and c looks at the wrong point in time.

stem: A and B, both Filipinos, got married in Tacloban City in 2005. Thereafter, A went to New York to work as a nurse, where he met C, also a Filipino citizen. In 2009, A obtained a divorce decree in New York. He became a citizen of New York in 2011. In 2012, A married C. In 2013, B married D in Tacloban City. Is the marriage between B and D valid?
choices: Valid, because a divorce decree was obtained by A, thus, capacitating B to remarry.
Void, because A and B were Filipinos at the time the marriage, therefore Article 26, par. 2 does not apply.
Valid, because when B married D, A was no longer a Filipino citizen.
Valid, because even if a Filipino was the one who obtained the divorce decree, it capacitated B to remarry D.
none of the above.
explanation: The B-D marriage is VOID, and none of a-d gives the right reason. Under Orbecido, what matters is citizenship when the divorce was obtained. A obtained the divorce in 2009 while still a Filipino and became a citizen of New York only in 2011, so the divorce does not capacitate B and B's marriage to D is bigamous (Arts. 35(4), 41). Choice b gives the outdated reason (citizenship at celebration). Choice d misreads Manalo: Manalo allows a divorce initiated by the FILIPINO spouse against an ALIEN spouse, but both spouses here were Filipinos at the time of the divorce, so Civil Code Art. 15 bars recognition.

stem: A and B, both Filipinos, got married in Tacloban City in 1991. Thereafter, A went to New York to work as a nurse where he met C, also a Filipino citizen. He became a citizen of New York in 1998. In 2001, A obtained a divorce decree in New York capacitating him to remarry. In 2002, A married C. In 2003, B married D in Tacloban City. Is the marriage between B and D valid?
choices: Void, because A and B were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, therefore Article 26, par. 2 does not apply.
Valid, because when B married D, A was no longer a Filipino citizen.
Void, because A was still a Filipino at the time the divorce decree was obtained, thus, did not capacitate B to remarry D.
Valid, because a divorce decree was obtained by A, thus capacitating B to remarry.
explanation: Under Republic v. Orbecido III (2005), citizenship is reckoned when the divorce is obtained. A became an American in 1998 and obtained the divorce in 2001, capacitating him to remarry. Under Art. 26(2), B, the Filipino spouse, has capacity to remarry. Choice a uses the outdated 'citizenship at the time of marriage' test. Choice c misstates the facts. Choice b points to the wrong time (B's remarriage). The divorce decree and A's national law must be proven, and the divorce judicially recognized in the Philippines (Garcia v. Recio; Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas).
key_note: Under current practice, B should first obtain judicial recognition of the foreign divorce before remarrying. The item tests the Orbecido reckoning point.

stem: In 1989, Maris, a Filipino citizen, married her boss Johnson, an American citizen, in Tokyo in a wedding ceremony celebrated according to Japanese laws. One (1) year later, Johnson returned to his native Nevada, and he validly obtained in that state an absolute divorce from his wife Maris. After Maris received the final judgment of divorce, she married her childhood sweetheart Pedro, also a Filipino citizen, in a religious ceremony in Cebu City, celebrated according to the formalities of Philippine law. Pedro later left for the United States and became naturalized as an American citizen. Maris followed Pedro to the United States, and after a serious quarrel, Maris filed a suit and obtained a divorce decree issued by the court in the state of Maryland. Maris then returned to the Philippines and in a civil ceremony celebrated in Cebu City according to the formalities of Philippine law, she married her former classmate Vincent likewise a Filipino citizen. Was the marriage of Maris and Johnson valid when celebrated? Is their marriage still validly existing now?
choices: Void when celebrated, because it was not solemnized under Philippine law.
Valid when celebrated, but no longer existing, having been dissolved by the divorce validly obtained by Johnson.
Valid and still existing, because Philippine law does not recognize divorce.
Valid when celebrated and still existing until Maris herself obtains a divorce.
explanation: Valid when celebrated: a marriage solemnized abroad in accordance with the laws of the place of celebration and valid there is valid here (Art. 26, par. 1). No longer existing: Johnson, the alien spouse, validly obtained an absolute divorce capacitating him to remarry. Under Art. 26, par. 2 the Filipino spouse, Maris, 'shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law'. The marriage was therefore dissolved, subject to judicial recognition of the divorce in a Philippine court.

stem: In 1989, Maris, a Filipino citizen, married her boss Johnson, an American citizen, in Tokyo in a wedding ceremony celebrated according to Japanese laws. One (1) year later, Johnson returned to his native Nevada, and he validly obtained in that state an absolute divorce from his wife Maris. After Maris received the final judgment of divorce, she married her childhood sweetheart Pedro, also a Filipino citizen, in a religious ceremony in Cebu City, celebrated according to the formalities of Philippine law. Pedro later left for the United States and became naturalized as an American citizen. Maris followed Pedro to the United States, and after a serious quarrel, Maris filed a suit and obtained a divorce decree issued by the court in the state of Maryland. Maris then returned to the Philippines and in a civil ceremony celebrated in Cebu City according to the formalities of Philippine law, she married her former classmate Vincent likewise a Filipino citizen. Was the marriage of Maris and Vincent valid when celebrated, and who is the lawful husband of Maris at this point in time?
choices: The marriage with Vincent is void for being bigamous; Pedro remains her lawful husband.
The marriage with Vincent is valid (subject to judicial recognition of the Maryland divorce); Vincent is her lawful husband.
The marriage with Vincent is voidable; Vincent is her lawful husband until annulment.
All her marriages after Johnson are void; Johnson remains her lawful husband.
explanation: Pedro was already a naturalized American when the Maryland divorce was obtained. Under Republic v. Orbecido III (2005), Art. 26(2) applies because citizenship is reckoned at the time of the divorce. Under Republic v. Manalo (2018), it does not matter that Maris, the Filipino spouse, initiated the divorce, so long as the divorce is valid under the alien spouse's national law and capacitates him to remarry. Maris was therefore capacitated to marry Vincent, assuming the divorce and the foreign law are proven and the divorce is judicially recognized. Vincent is her lawful husband.
key_note: Note: the bar reviewers' key (written before Orbecido and Manalo) marked the Vincent marriage void and Pedro as the lawful husband; this is incorrect under current law, because citizenship is reckoned at the time of divorce (Orbecido) and the Filipino spouse may be the one who obtains the divorce (Manalo).

stem: Flor and Virgilio were married to each other in Roxas City in 1980. In 1984, Flor was offered a teaching job in Canada, which she accepted. In 1989, she applied for and was granted Canadian citizenship. The following year, she sued for divorce from Virgilio in a Canadian court. After Virgilio was served with summons, the Canadian court tried the case and decreed the divorce. Shortly thereafter, Flor married a Canadian. Can Virgilio marry again in the Philippines?
choices: No, because both were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, so Art. 26 does not apply.
Yes, because Flor was already a foreigner when she obtained the divorce.
No, because divorce is contrary to public policy.
Yes, but only after a declaration of presumptive death.
explanation: Yes. Flor was a naturalized Canadian when she obtained the divorce. Under Republic v. Orbecido III (2005), Art. 26(2) applies even if both spouses were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, because the reckoning point is citizenship when the divorce is obtained. Virgilio, the Filipino spouse, acquires capacity to remarry once the Canadian divorce, and Flor's capacity to remarry under Canadian law, are proven and judicially recognized in the Philippines. A declaration of presumptive death (d) applies only to an absent spouse.
key_note: Note: the bar reviewers' key marked a (No, both were Filipinos at the time of marriage); this is incorrect because Republic v. Orbecido III (2005) reckons citizenship at the time the divorce is obtained.

stem: Harry married Wilma, a very wealthy woman. Barely five (5) years into the marriage, Wilma fell in love with Joseph. Thus, Wilma went to a small country in Europe, became a naturalized citizen of that country, divorced Harry, and married Joseph. A year thereafter, Wilma and Joseph returned and established permanent residence in the Philippines. Harry tells you that he has fallen in love with another woman, Elizabeth, and wants to marry her because, after all, Wilma is already married to Joseph. Can Harry legally marry Elizabeth?
choices: No, because Harry and Wilma were both Filipinos when they married.
Yes, immediately, because Wilma already remarried.
Yes, after he obtains judicial recognition of the foreign divorce obtained by Wilma, then a foreigner.
No, unless he first secures a declaration of nullity under Art. 36.
explanation: Yes, but only after judicial recognition of the foreign divorce. Wilma was already a naturalized foreign citizen when she divorced Harry. Under Republic v. Orbecido III (2005), Art. 26(2) applies even though both were Filipinos at the time of the marriage, so Harry, the Filipino spouse, acquires capacity to remarry. Wilma's remarriage does not by itself free Harry (b). He must have the divorce decree and Wilma's national law proven and recognized in a Philippine court (Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas, 2010; Garcia v. Recio, 2001). Art. 36 (d) is unrelated.

stem: In 1985, Sonny and Lulu, both Filipino citizens, were married in the Philippines. In 1987, they separated, and Sonny went to Canada, where he obtained a divorce in the same year. He then married another Filipina, Auring, in Canada on 01 Jan. 1988. They had two sons, James and John. In 1990, after failing to hear from Sonny, Lulu married Tirso, by whom she had a daughter, Verna. In 1991, Sonny visited the Philippines where he succumbed to heart attack. Discuss the effect of the divorce obtained by Sonny in Canada.
choices: It dissolved the marriage, since it was valid in Canada where it was obtained.
It capacitated Lulu to remarry under Art. 26(2), FC.
It has no effect, because both spouses were Filipino citizens at the time; their marriage subsisted.
It converted the marriage into a voidable one.
explanation: The divorce had no effect. Sonny and Lulu were both Filipino citizens when Sonny obtained the divorce in Canada. Under Civil Code Art. 15, laws on family rights and duties and on status bind Filipinos even abroad, so a divorce between two Filipinos is not recognized here (Tenchavez v. Escaño; Garcia v. Recio). Art. 26(2) does not apply because neither spouse was an alien when the divorce was obtained. The marriage subsisted. Sonny's marriage to Auring (January 1, 1988, before the Family Code took effect) is void as bigamous under Civil Code Art. 83. Lulu's 1990 marriage to Tirso is void as bigamous under FC Arts. 35(4) and 41, since she did not obtain a judicial declaration of presumptive death (and four years of absence had not even elapsed).

stem: Marvin, a Filipino, and Shelley, an American, both residents of California, decided to get married in their local parish. Two years after their marriage, Shelley obtained a divorce in California. While in Boracay, Marvin met Manel, a Filipina, who was vacationing there. Marvin fell in love with her. After a brief courtship and complying with all the requirements, they got married in Hongkong to avoid publicity, it being Marvin's second marriage. Is his marriage to Manel valid?
choices: No, because Marvin's first marriage subsists; divorce is not recognized.
Yes, because the divorce obtained by Shelley, the alien spouse, capacitated Marvin to remarry under Art. 26(2).
No, because they married abroad to avoid publicity.
Yes, because the marriage is valid in Hongkong regardless of Marvin's capacity.
explanation: Valid. The Marvin-Shelley marriage, celebrated in California and valid there, is valid here (Art. 26, par. 1). Shelley, the alien spouse, then validly obtained a divorce in California capacitating her to remarry. Under Art. 26, par. 2, Marvin, the Filipino spouse, acquired capacity to remarry. His marriage to Manel, solemnized in Hong Kong in compliance with all requirements, is valid if valid there (Art. 26, par. 1) and is not bigamous. Marrying abroad to avoid publicity has no legal effect. Marvin should have the divorce judicially recognized for it to have effect in Philippine records.

stem: Eka, a Filipina, and Du-guil, a Korean, married in the Philippines. Thereafter, they moved to Seoul, South Korea. While there, Du-guil began to ignore Eka. He was always out with his friends and usually came home drunk. When Eka could not take their marital situation anymore, she asked for a divorce. Du-guil agreed on the condition that Eka would be the one to file for divorce, and that the ground should be "no fault", meaning, neither of them is at fault or neither would be accused of any wrongdoing. After the divorce, Eka went back to the Philippines and filed a case to have the judgment of divorce recognized. The RTC denied Eka's petition because she alone filed for divorce, in violation of Art. 26(2) of the Family Code. According to the RTC, Art. 26 requires that either the foreign spouse alone initiates the filing of the divorce or, at the very least, Eka and Du-guil should have filed for divorce jointly. Is the RTC correct?
choices: Yes, because Art. 26(2) requires that the divorce be obtained by the alien spouse.
Yes, because a divorce obtained solely by the Filipino spouse is contrary to Art. 15 of the Civil Code.
No, because Art. 26(2) applies regardless of whether the divorce was initiated by the foreign spouse, jointly, or by the Filipino spouse alone.
No, because a no-fault divorce is always recognized in the Philippines without need of judicial recognition.
explanation: The RTC is wrong. In Republic v. Manalo (G.R. No. 221029, April 24, 2018, En Banc), the Court held that Art. 26(2) requires only that a divorce be 'validly obtained abroad'. It does not matter who initiated the proceeding, so long as the divorce capacitates the alien spouse to remarry. Galapon v. Republic (2020) and Abel v. Rule (2021) reiterate that Art. 26(2) applies whether the divorce is obtained by the foreign spouse, jointly, or solely by the Filipino spouse. Eka may have the divorce recognized upon proof of the decree and Korean law. Choice d is wrong because judicial recognition is always required.

stem: A divorce decree obtained abroad may only be recognized if it is obtained by a Filipino?
choices: True
False
explanation: False. Under Art. 26(2) as construed in Republic v. Manalo (2018), a foreign divorce in a mixed marriage may be recognized whether it was obtained by the alien spouse (as in Pilapil v. Ibay-Somera, where the German husband obtained it) or by the Filipino spouse, so long as it was validly obtained abroad and capacitated the alien spouse to remarry. A divorce obtained by a Filipino against another Filipino is NOT recognized (Civil Code Art. 15). Recognition does not depend on which spouse obtained the decree.
key_note: The transcript of this recitation question appears garbled (likely 'only if obtained by the foreign spouse'). Under either reading the answer is False under Manalo.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Where a marriage between a Filipino citizen and a foreigner is validly celebrated and a divorce is thereafter validly obtained abroad by the alien spouse capacitating him or her to remarry, the Filipino spouse shall have capacity to remarry under Philippine law.

2. If it is the Filipino spouse in a mixed marriage who obtains the divorce abroad against the alien spouse, the divorce will not be recognized in the Philippines and the Filipino spouse cannot remarry under Philippine law.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is the text of FC Art. 26, par. 2 (added by E.O. 227), so it is true. Tolentino (PDF p. 162, book p. 263) states the view in No. 2 and criticizes it as placing the Filipino on a plane of inequality. That view is now outdated: Republic v. Manalo (G.R. No. 221029, April 24, 2018, En Banc) held that Art. 26(2) applies even if it was the Filipino spouse who initiated and obtained the divorce abroad, provided it was validly obtained and capacitated the alien spouse to remarry. No. 2 is false under current law. The decree and the alien spouse's national law must still be proven and the divorce judicially recognized.

stem: Under Article 26 of the Family Code, when a foreign spouse divorces his/her Filipino spouse, the latter may re-marry by proving only that the foreign spouse has obtained a divorce against her or him abroad.
choices: True
False
explanation: False. Under Garcia v. Recio (G.R. No. 138322, Oct. 2, 2001), the Filipino spouse must prove not only that the alien spouse obtained a divorce abroad, but also that the divorce is valid under the alien's national law and capacitated the alien spouse to remarry. Art. 26(2) requires a divorce 'validly obtained abroad ... capacitating him or her to remarry'. Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign laws or judgments, so both the decree and the national law must be alleged and proven, and the divorce judicially recognized (Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas, 2010).
key_note: The UP BOC answer also notes an alternative answer (True), reading Art. 26(2) as making the divorce itself sufficient. The main answer follows Garcia v. Recio.

stem: Ted, married to Annie, went to Canada to work. Five (5) years later, Ted became a naturalized Canadian citizen. He returned to the Philippines to convince Annie to settle in Canada. Unfortunately, Ted discovered that Annie and his friend Louie were having an affair. Deeply hurt, Ted returned to Canada and filed a petition for divorce which was granted. In December 2013, Ted decided to marry his childhood friend Corazon in the Philippines. In preparation for the wedding, Ted went to the Local Civil Registry of Quezon City where his marriage contract with Annie was registered. He asked the Civil Register to annotate the decree of divorce on his marriage contract with Annie. However, he was advised by the National Statistics Office (NSO) to file a petition for judicial recognition of the decree of divorce in the Philippines. Is it necessary for Ted to file a petition for judicial recognition of the decree of divorce he obtained in Canada before he can contract a second marriage in the Philippines?
choices: No, because Ted is already a Canadian citizen and is not bound by Philippine law.
Yes, because a foreign divorce decree has no effect in the Philippines until judicially recognized, upon proof of the decree and the foreign law.
No, because the civil registrar may annotate a foreign divorce decree administratively.
Yes, because divorce obtained by a former Filipino is never recognized in the Philippines.
explanation: Yes. A foreign divorce decree, even if validly obtained, has no effect in the Philippines until it is judicially recognized in an appropriate proceeding. Philippine courts do not take judicial notice of foreign judgments and laws. Ted must prove the fact of divorce by an official copy, the jurisdiction of the Canadian court, and Canadian law on divorce (Corpuz v. Sto. Tomas, G.R. No. 186571, Aug. 11, 2010; Rule 108; Rule 39, Sec. 48). The civil registrar cannot annotate the decree administratively without a court order. D is wrong: a divorce obtained by a former Filipino who was already an alien is recognizable (Orbecido).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. For a marriage in a remote place to be exempt from the license requirement, the habitual residence of the female must be at least fifteen kilometers from the municipal building, besides the absence of means of transportation.

2. In case either or both of the contracting parties are at the point of death, the marriage may be solemnized without necessity of a marriage license and shall remain valid even if the ailing party subsequently survives.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. Under FC Art. 28, the marriage may be solemnized without a license if the residence of EITHER party is so located that there is no means of transportation to appear personally before the local civil registrar. Civil Code Art. 72 also required that the female's habitual residence be at least 15 kilometers from the municipal building, but the Family Code dropped this, and the handicap may be that of the male or the female (Tolentino, book pp. 265-266). No. 2 is true: it reproduces Art. 27. If the party was actually at the point of death, his later recovery does not affect validity.

src: Uribe samplex – Midterm Exam (scanned); Uribe samplex MCQ set (Studocu, 'kuya R' version)
stem: X, a Roman Catholic, and Y, a Baptist had been living together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage since January 1, 2006, although both are capacitated to marry each other. On March 1, 2011, in a birthday party in Quezon City, X suffered a heart attack. Believing that X was about to die, Y asked Z, a parish priest of Palo, Leyte to solemnize her marriage to X. Z solemnized the marriage. Today, X is still practicing his profession. Is the marriage valid?
choices: Void, because the priest had no authority to solemnize marriages in Quezon City.
Void, because of the lack of a marriage license.
Void, because X survived the heart attack.
Valid despite the absence of a marriage license because X subsequently survived.
Valid despite the absence of a marriage license because they have been living together as husband and wife since January 1, 2006.
explanation: From January 1, 2006 to March 1, 2011, X and Y, both capacitated, lived together as husband and wife for more than five years. Their marriage is therefore exempt from the license requirement under Art. 34, and it is independently exempt as a marriage in articulo mortis under Art. 27. A priest's authority (Art. 7(2)) is not limited to his parish or territory. X is a Roman Catholic, which satisfies the membership proviso, and venue does not matter for a marriage at the point of death (Art. 8). Choice d gives the wrong reason: the marriage is valid whether or not X survived, not because he survived (Art. 27).

stem: X, a Roman Catholic, and Y, a Baptist, had been living together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage since April 1, 2006, although both are capacitated to marry each other. On March 1, 2011, in a birthday party in Quezon City, X suffered a heart attack. Believing that X was about to die, Y asked Z, a parish priest of Palo, Leyte to solemnize her marriage to X. Z solemnized the marriage. Today, X is still practicing his profession. Is the marriage valid, voidable or void?
choices: Valid despite the absence of a marriage license because X subsequently survived.
Valid despite the absence of a marriage license because they have been living together as husband and wife since April 1, 2006.
Void, because the priest had no authority to solemnize marriage in Quezon City
Void because of the lack of a marriage license.
None of the above.
explanation: Valid, but none of a-d gives the right reason. Under Art. 27, a marriage in articulo mortis may be solemnized without a license and 'shall remain valid even if the ailing party subsequently survives'. It is valid because X was at the point of death when it was solemnized, not because he survived, so a is wrong. From April 1, 2006 to March 1, 2011 is less than five years, so Art. 34 does not apply and b is wrong. A priest's authority is not territorial (c), and d ignores the articulo mortis exemption. (Uribe agreed with e in the class discussion.)

stem: Isidro and Irma, Filipinos, both 18 years of age, were passengers of Flight No. 317 of Oriental Airlines. The plane they boarded was of Philippine registry. While en route from Manila to Greece some passengers hijacked the plane, held the chief pilot hostage at the cockpit and ordered him to fly instead to Libya. During the hijacking Isidro suffered a heart attack and was on the verge of death. Since Irma was already eight months pregnant by Isidro, she pleaded to the hijackers to allow the assistant pilot to solemnize her marriage with Isidro. Soon after the marriage, Isidro expired. As the plane landed in Libya Irma gave birth. However, the baby died a few minutes after complete delivery. Back in the Philippines Irma immediately filed a claim for inheritance. The parents of Isidro opposed her claim contending that the marriage between her and Isidro was void ab initio on the following grounds: (a) They had not given their consent to the marriage of their son; (b) There was no marriage license; (c) The solemnizing officer had no authority to perform the marriage; and (d) The solemnizing officer did not file an affidavit of marriage with the proper civil registrar. Which contention is correctly resolved?
choices: The marriage is void because the parents of the 18-year-old parties did not consent.
The marriage is void for lack of a marriage license.
The marriage is void because only the chief pilot, not the assistant pilot, may solemnize marriages in articulo mortis.

None of the contentions renders the marriage void: lack of parental consent makes it voidable, the in articulo mortis marriage is license-exempt, the assistant pilot acting for the disabled chief pilot had authority, and non-filing of the affidavit is a mere irregularity.
explanation: (a) Isidro and Irma, both 18, lacked parental consent, which makes the marriage voidable, not void (Arts. 14, 45(1)). (b) A marriage in articulo mortis between passengers or crew members is exempt from the license requirement (Arts. 27, 31). (c) The bar answer treats the assistant pilot, acting for an airplane chief held hostage, as authorized under Arts. 7(3) and 31 given the extraordinary circumstances. Even on a strict view, Art. 35(2) would save the marriage if either party believed in good faith that he had authority. (d) The solemnizing officer's failure to file the affidavit (Arts. 29-30) is a mere irregularity (Art. 4, par. 3). None of the contentions makes the marriage void.
key_note: Contention (c) is debatable. Arts. 7(3) and 31 name only the airplane chief or pilot, and Uribe teaches that a first officer has no authority. The bar suggested answer rests on the chief pilot's disability. The other three resolutions are settled.

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. A marriage in articulo mortis between passengers or crew members may be solemnized by a ship captain or by an airplane pilot not only while the ship is at sea or the plane is in flight, but also during stopovers at ports of call.
2. A military commander of a unit who is a commissioned officer may solemnize marriages in articulo mortis only between members of the armed forces within the zone of military operation.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is true: it reproduces FC Art. 31. No. 2 is false: Art. 32 authorizes a military commander of a unit who is a commissioned officer to solemnize marriages in articulo mortis 'between persons within the zone of military operation, whether members of the armed forces or CIVILIANS'. Under Art. 7(4) he may act only in the absence of the chaplain assigned to the unit. Tolentino notes that the Civil Code limited this authority to time of war, while the Family Code speaks of military operations (book p. 267).

stem: Consider the statement true only when it is absolutely true.
statements: 1. Under present law, a marriage between members of an ethnic cultural community, one of whom is sixteen years old, is valid if solemnized in accordance with their customs, rites or practices.

2. Marriages among Muslims or among members of the ethnic cultural communities may be performed validly without the necessity of a marriage license, provided they are solemnized in accordance with their customs, rites or practices.
choices: Both are true
Both are false
No. 1 is true, No. 2 is false
No. 1 is false, No. 2 is true
explanation: No. 1 is false. The license exemption in Art. 33 does not dispense with the essential requisites (Art. 2). Tolentino (book pp. 267-268), citing People v. Mora Dumpo, suggested the age requirement might yield to non-Christian customs, but that view is outdated. R.A. 11596 (2021) declares child marriages, where a party is below 18, void ab initio and penalizes them, and after its one-year transition period it applies to Muslim and indigenous communities as well. No. 2 is true: it reproduces Art. 33. The Civil Code (Art. 78) gave this privilege only to non-Christians living in non-Christian provinces, and the Family Code removed that limit. Muslim marriages are also governed by P.D. 1083.

stem: No license shall be necessary for the marriage of a man and a woman who have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years and without any legal impediment to marry each other.
choices: True
False
explanation: This reproduces the first sentence of FC Art. 34. The parties must state these facts in an affidavit before any person authorized to administer oaths, and the solemnizing officer must state under oath that he ascertained their qualifications and found no legal impediment. Under Niñal v. Bayadog (2000) and Manzano v. Sanchez (2001), the five years must immediately precede the marriage, be continuous and exclusive, and be free of any legal impediment throughout, and there must be no impediment at the time of the marriage.

stem: If X died in 1987, the marriage between X and Y may be valid even if there was no marriage license if they cohabited as husband and wife for six years prior to the marriage and their cohabitation was not entirely free from legal impediment.
choices: True
False
explanation: X died in 1987, so the X-Y marriage was celebrated under the Civil Code. Civil Code Art. 76 exempted from the license requirement a man and a woman of age who, 'being unmarried, have lived together as husband and wife for at least five years'. Niñal v. Bayadog (2000) requires that the five-year period, counted back from the day of the marriage, be free of legal impediment. If the parties cohabited for six years and the impediment existed only at the start, the five years immediately before the marriage may have been impediment-free. The marriage therefore MAY be valid without a license.
key_note: Note: the class answer key marked this False (on the view that Niñal requires the whole cohabitation to be impediment-free); this is incorrect because only the five years immediately before the marriage count, as Uribe himself explained in the discussion. Watch the word 'may'.

stem: A and B were married. During the subsistence of their marriage, A left the conjugal abode and lived with C as husband and wife. Six years later, B died. Two years after B's death, A and C, who continued to live together, were married under the Family Code without a marriage license, executing an affidavit under Article 34 that they had lived together as husband and wife for at least five years. A died yesterday, and the heirs of B assail the validity of the marriage of A and C for lack of a marriage license. The marriage of A and C is:
choices: Valid, because A and C had cohabited for eight years and had no legal impediment at the time of their marriage
Void, because the five-year cohabitation under Article 34 must itself be free of any legal impediment, and A was still married to B during most of that period
Voidable, because the affidavit under Article 34 was false
Valid, because a false Article 34 affidavit is a mere irregularity in a formal requisite
None of the above
explanation: Uribe's answer (2025 recitation): VALID. Under FC Art. 34, as Uribe reads Borja-Manzano v. Sanchez (2001), the exemption requires at least five years of cohabitation as husband and wife and no legal impediment at the time of the marriage. B was already dead when A and C married, so there was no impediment at the time of solemnization, and the marriage is valid without a license. Uribe distinguished the Civil Code: if the Civil Code governed (Art. 76, 'being unmarried'), Niñal v. Bayadog would make the marriage void.
key_note: Contrary (stricter) view: Niñal v. Bayadog, Manzano v. Sanchez as commonly read, and Republic v. Dayot (2008) require the five-year cohabitation itself to be exclusive, continuous and free of impediment, which would make this marriage void. For Uribe's quiz, answer VALID (his stated teaching) and mention the strict view in essays.

stem: Roderick and Faye were high school sweethearts. When Roderick was 18 and Faye, 16 years old, they started to live together as husband and wife without the benefit of marriage. When Faye reached 18 years of age, her parents forcibly took her back and arranged for her marriage to Brad. Although Faye lived with Brad after the marriage, Roderick continued to regularly visit Faye while Brad was away at work. During their marriage, Faye gave birth to a baby girl, Laica. When Faye was 25 years old, Brad discovered her continued liaison with Roderick and in one of their heated arguments, Faye shot Brad to death. She lost no time in marrying her true love Roderick, without a marriage license, claiming that they have been continuously cohabiting for more than 5 years. Was the marriage of Roderick and Faye valid?
choices: Valid, since they had cohabited for more than 5 years, exempting them from a license under Art. 34.
Valid, since a license is a mere formal requisite.
Void, because there was no marriage license and they were not exempt: no 5 continuous years of cohabitation without legal impediment.

explanation: Void. Art. 34 requires at least five years of cohabitation as husband and wife, immediately before the marriage, that is continuous, exclusive and free of any legal impediment throughout (Niñal v. Bayadog; Manzano v. Sanchez; Republic v. Dayot). Here Faye was below 18 when the cohabitation began, then married Brad, and saw Roderick only on occasional visits. That is not cohabitation as husband and wife, and her subsisting marriage to Brad was a legal impediment. With no license and no valid exemption, the marriage is void (Art. 35(3)). (Faye's killing of Brad may also raise the Art. 38(9) impediment.)
